title: Bloom Filters & Sketches
subtitle: Watch a tiny bit array skip useless disk reads, then see how two more sketches count events and unique users in kilobytes.
learn: How a Bloom filter answers 'definitely not here' or 'maybe here' using bits and hashes
Why false positives happen, why false negatives do not, and how bits per key set the error rate
How a filter in front of a database or cache avoids reads for keys that do not exist
How a Count-Min sketch estimates how often something happened, and which way it errs
How HyperLogLog counts unique items with about 12 KB, and why sketches merge across servers

steps.title: Asking for things that are not there
steps.body: A lookup service gets 1,000 requests for user IDs that do not exist: typos, scrapers guessing IDs, stale links. Without help, each one misses the cache (or has none), then reads the disk to learn there is nothing to find. Every one of those reads is wasted work. Can we answer 'not here' cheaply, without storing every key in memory?
steps.idea: Lookups for absent keys are pure waste: they pay the full read path and return nothing.
steps.caption: Every absent key still costs a disk read.

steps.title: A Bloom filter: bits and hashes
steps.body: A Bloom filter is an array of bits, all 0 at the start. To add a key, run it through k different hash functions and set the k bits they point to. For 1 million keys we use about 10 million bits, roughly 1.25 MB, and k = 7. The keys themselves are never stored, only their fingerprints in the bits. The filter lives in memory next to the caller or inside the database engine, so checking it costs nanoseconds, not a network call. It must be loaded with every key that exists and updated on every insert, or a real key will be wrongly rejected.
steps.idea: Adding a key flips k bits to 1; the filter stores no keys, only bit patterns.
steps.caption: Each new key sets 7 bits in the filter.

steps.title: A 'no' is always true
steps.body: To check a key, hash it the same k ways and look at those bits. If even one bit is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set that bit. The filter says 'definitely not present' and the app skips the disk entirely. Bits are never cleared, so this answer can never be wrong.
steps.idea: One zero bit proves absence: Bloom filters have no false negatives.
steps.caption: A zero bit means: skip the disk read.

steps.title: A 'yes' only means maybe
steps.body: If all k bits are 1, the key may have been added, or other keys may have set those same bits by coincidence. The filter says 'maybe present', so the app must still check the real store. When that check finds nothing, we have a false positive. It costs one wasted read, which is the price of the whole scheme.
steps.idea: All-ones means 'maybe': the filter can wrongly say yes, never wrongly say no.
steps.caption: A false positive costs one wasted disk read.

steps.title: Sizing the filter
steps.body: Error rate depends on bits per key. As a rule of thumb with the best k, about 5 bits per key gives roughly 10% false positives, 10 bits gives about 1%, and 14 to 15 bits gives about 0.1%. At 10 bits per key, our 1,000 absent lookups drop from 1,000 disk reads to about 10. Memory is paid once; every lookup for an absent key then skips the disk. If most lookups find their key, the filter helps little. The same filter in front of a cache stops absent-key lookups falling through to the database on every request (cache penetration).
steps.idea: Each extra 5 bits per key cuts false positives roughly ten-fold, at linear memory cost.
steps.caption: 10 bits per key: about 1 in 100 slips through.

steps.title: What a Bloom filter cannot do
steps.body: You cannot delete a key, because clearing its bits could erase bits shared with other keys and create false negatives. You cannot list the keys or read a value back. And if you add far more keys than you sized for, more bits fill up and false positives climb. Variants such as counting Bloom filters or cuckoo filters add deletion, and many systems simply rebuild the filter periodically.
steps.idea: Size for the expected key count; a filter only grows more wrong as it fills, and it cannot forget.
steps.caption: Deleting a key is not supported.

steps.title: Count-Min sketch: how often?
steps.body: A different question: how many times did each video get viewed? A Count-Min sketch is a small grid, say 5 rows by 2,719 counters. For every event, hash the item once per row and add 1 to one counter in each row. With those dimensions, memory is about 54 KB of 4-byte counters, no matter how many distinct videos exist.
steps.idea: A Count-Min sketch keeps approximate counts for unlimited items in fixed memory.
steps.caption: Each event increments one counter per row.

steps.title: Reading a count: take the minimum
steps.body: To estimate a count, hash the item in each row and take the smallest of the 5 counters. Other items collide into the same counters and only ever add to them, so every counter is at least the true count. The minimum is the least inflated one. The estimate can be too high but never too low, by at most about 0.1% of total events with 99% confidence (the grid is sized for that), so rare items can look far more popular than they are; Count-Min is best for finding frequent items.
steps.idea: Count-Min overestimates, never underestimates; the minimum across rows trims the damage.
steps.caption: Estimate = smallest counter across rows.

steps.title: HyperLogLog: how many different?
steps.body: Counting unique visitors exactly needs a set of every ID: a billion 8-byte IDs is about 8 GB before any set overhead. HyperLogLog hashes each ID and watches for rare patterns such as many leading zero bits; seeing one with 20 zeros suggests about a million distinct items were hashed. It splits items into 16,384 buckets and combines them with a harmonic mean (a plain average would be thrown off by outliers), giving about 0.8% error in 12 KB. Two HyperLogLogs from different servers merge by taking the max of each bucket when both use the same hash and bucket count.
steps.idea: HyperLogLog estimates unique counts in about 12 KB and merges cleanly across machines.
steps.caption: Unique users counted in 12 KB.

steps.title: Pick the sketch by the question
steps.body: Is this key in the set? Use a Bloom filter: no is certain, yes is maybe. How many times did this item occur? Use Count-Min: counts can be high, never low. How many distinct items were there? Use HyperLogLog: a small relative error. All three trade a little accuracy for far less memory than storing every key or count. Bloom and Count-Min err in one direction; HyperLogLog can err either way. Use them where an approximate answer is acceptable, never where you need exactness.
steps.idea: Sketches trade a small, bounded error for far less memory than exact structures: Count-Min and HyperLogLog stay fixed in size, and a Bloom filter needs only about 10 bits per key.
steps.caption: Three questions, three small structures.

quiz.q: A Bloom filter in front of a database answers 'no' for a key. What should the app do?
options: Query the database anyway to confirm
Retry the filter with different hash functions
Skip the database: the key is definitely absent
Add the key to the filter and carry on
quiz.why: A 'no' means at least one required bit is 0. Since bits are never cleared, the key was never added. Bloom filters have no false negatives.

quiz.q: A filter with a 1% false-positive rate guards a store. 1,000,000 lookups arrive, all for keys that do not exist. About how many disk reads happen?
options: Zero, since the filter is exact
quiz.why: Only false positives pass through the filter, so about 1% of 1,000,000 = 10,000 reads, instead of 1,000,000 without the filter.

quiz.q: Your Count-Min sketch says an item occurred 5,300 times. Which statement is correct?
options: The true count is at most 5,300, possibly less
The true count may be above or below 5,300 equally
The true count is at least 5,300, possibly more
quiz.why: Collisions only add to counters, so estimates are never below the true count. The true count is therefore at most 5,300.

quiz.q: Fifty servers each track unique daily visitors. You need one global unique count without shipping all IDs. Which fits best?
options: A Bloom filter per server, summing the 'yes' answers
A Count-Min sketch per server, summing the counters
A plain counter per server, added together
A HyperLogLog per server, merged by taking the max of each bucket
quiz.why: Visitors seen on several servers would be double-counted by a plain sum. HyperLogLogs merge by per-bucket max, which removes duplicates, in about 12 KB each.

cheatsheet.def: Bit array plus k hashes. Answers 'definitely not in set' or 'maybe in set'. No false negatives, some false positives, no deletes.
Rule of thumb with best k: about 10% at 5 bits per key, 1% at 10, 0.1% at about 14-15. Optimal k is about 0.7 times bits per key.
In front of disk reads (e.g. LSM-tree database files), caches, and databases, so lookups for absent keys skip the expensive read.
Grid of counters with one hash per row. Add: +1 in each row. Estimate: min across rows. Overestimates only.
The most frequent items. Count-Min plus a small top-N list finds trending items without a counter per item.
Estimates distinct count from leading-zero patterns of hashes. About 12 KB gives roughly 0.8% error, for billions of items.
Bloom filters merge by OR, Count-Min by adding counters, HyperLogLog by max per bucket, so shards can be combined (Bloom and Count-Min need same size and hashes).
When you need exact answers, deletion, or the actual keys: money, inventory, billing, access control.
